topics.title: Words for time
topics.intro: Historians use special words to talk about time. Knowing them makes every history topic easier.
topics.teach: Explain what BC and AD mean.
topics.talk: Ask her which century we are in, and why it isn’t the 20th.
topics.hook: **BC** counts down towards year 1, **AD** counts up from it. There is no year 0: 1 BC is followed straight by AD 1.

topics.title: Which century?
topics.teach: Explain why 1900 is in the 19th century.
topics.talk: Ask her which century the Great Fire of London (1666) was in.
topics.hook: Add one to the hundreds: 1666 → 16 + 1 = **17th** century. A year ending in 00 belongs to the century that is just finishing.

topics.title: The big timeline of Britain
topics.intro: A secure mental timeline is the backbone of history. We’ll build it period by period, from the Stone Age to today.
topics.teach: Put the Romans, Vikings and Tudors in order and say roughly when each was.
topics.talk: Ask her to put three periods in order: Victorians, Romans, Tudors.
topics.hook: “Willie, Willie, Harry, Stee, Harry, Dick, John, Harry three…”: the old rhyme that lists every monarch since 1066, in order.

topics.title: The earliest civilisations
topics.intro: Long before Roman Britain, great civilisations grew up along rivers: in Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and China. Ancient Greece came a little later.
topics.teach: Explain why early civilisations grew up near rivers.
topics.talk: Ask her what the Greeks gave us that we still use today.
topics.hook: Civilisations are born by rivers: **Nile** (Egypt), **Tigris and Euphrates** (Mesopotamia), **Indus** (India), **Yellow River** (China).

topics.title: Beyond Europe: Baghdad, the Maya and Benin
topics.intro: While Britain was in the Anglo-Saxon and medieval periods, other parts of the world had great cities and kingdoms.
topics.teach: Explain why Baghdad around AD 900 was a centre of learning.
topics.talk: Ask her what the House of Wisdom was.
topics.hook: Books, maths and brass: Baghdad’s **House of Wisdom**, the **Maya** zero and the **Benin** Bronzes.

topics.title: 1066: the year of three battles
topics.intro: When Edward the Confessor died in January 1066 without a child, several men claimed the English throne. This is the start of Year 7 history.
topics.teach: Explain the most important reason William won at Hastings.
topics.talk: Ask her who the claimants to the throne were in 1066.
topics.hook: 1066: the year of **three kings** (Edward, Harold, William) and **three battles** (Fulford, Stamford Bridge, Hastings).

topics.title: How the Normans took control
topics.intro: William had won a battle, but now he had to control a whole country of about two million English people.
topics.teach: Explain how castles helped William control England.
topics.talk: Ask her what the Domesday Book was for.
topics.hook: William’s toolkit: **castles** to frighten, the **feudal system** to bind everyone to the king, **Domesday** to count it all.

items.prompt: What does BC stand for?
items.explain: BC means “Before Christ”: years counted backwards from the traditional birth year of Jesus. Some books use BCE (Before Common Era).
items.hook: BC counts **down** towards year 1, so 500 BC is longer ago than 100 BC.
items.example: Museum labels saying “c. 3000 BC” mean about 5000 years ago: roughly when Stonehenge was begun.

items.prompt: What does AD stand for?
items.explain: AD stands for Anno Domini, Latin for “in the year of the Lord”. Some books use CE (Common Era).
items.hook: “Anno” is like “annual”: it means year. Anno Domini = “in the year of the Lord”, counting forwards.
items.example: Look for “A.D.” carved with the date on old buildings, foundation stones and gravestones.

items.prompt: How many years are in a century?
items.explain: A century is 100 years.
items.hook: **Cent** = 100: 100 cents in a dollar, 100 centimetres in a metre, and a centipede is named for “100 legs”.
items.example: In cricket, when a batter scores 100 runs it is called a “century”.

items.prompt: How many years are in a decade?
items.explain: A decade is 10 years (the 1960s is a decade).
items.hook: **Dec** = 10: a decagon has 10 sides, and December was the 10th month of the old Roman year.
items.example: The 1960s, the 1990s and the 2010s are each a decade.

items.prompt: How many years are in a millennium?
items.explain: A millennium is 1000 years.
items.hook: **Mille** = 1000 in Latin: a millimetre is a thousandth of a metre, and a millipede is named for “1000 legs”.
items.example: London’s Millennium Bridge and the Millennium Dome (now the O2) were built to mark the year 2000.

items.prompt: What does “c.” mean in front of a date, as in c. 1200?
items.explain: “c.” is short for “circa”, Latin for “around”. We use it when we don’t know the exact date.
items.hook: **Circa** sounds like circle: we are circling around the date, close but not exactly on it.
items.example: Museum labels often say things like “c. 1500” when nobody knows the exact year an object was made.

items.prompt: What is the word for putting events in time order?
items.explain: Chronology means the order in which events happened (chron = time).
items.hook: **Chron** = time (from Greek): chronological order, synchronise your watches, a chronometer is a clock.
items.example: The photos on a phone are shown in chronological order: oldest to newest, or newest first.

items.prompt: Which word describes the period in Europe from about AD 500 to 1500?
items.explain: “Medieval” means the Middle Ages, roughly AD 500 to 1500.
items.hook: **Medi** = middle, as in medium: the **Middle** Ages sit in the middle, between the ancient and modern worlds.
items.example: Medieval castles such as Warwick, Conwy and Bodiam can still be visited today.

items.prompt: What do we call the time before people wrote things down?
items.explain: Prehistory is the time before written records. In Britain this includes the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages.
items.hook: **Pre** = before, as in preview: prehistory is the time **before** history was written down.
items.example: Stonehenge is prehistoric: nobody left any writing to tell us exactly why it was built.

items.prompt: What is a source from the time being studied called?
items.explain: A primary source was made at the time (a diary, a coin, a photograph). A secondary source was made later (a textbook).
items.hook: **Primary** = first-hand, made at the time. **Secondary** = second-hand, made later.
items.example: A Victorian photo of your street is a primary source; a modern website about the Victorians is secondary.

items.prompt: What is the study of the past through objects dug up from the ground called?
items.explain: Archaeologists study the past from physical remains such as tools, bones and buildings.
items.hook: **Archae** = ancient (like “archaic”): archaeologists dig up the past, layer by layer.
items.example: The Sutton Hoo ship burial in Suffolk was dug up in 1939; its famous helmet is in the British Museum.

items.prompt: Which century are we living in now?

options.feedback: The 20th century was 1901–2000. Years starting 20.. are in the 21st century.
Centuries are counted in hundreds of years, so we are only in the 21st.

items.explain: The 21st century runs from 2001 to 2100.
items.hook: Like birthdays: when you are 10, you are in your 11th year. So the 2000s are the **21st** century.
items.example: The year 2000 was the last year of the 20th century; you were born in the 21st.

items.prompt: Put these periods of British history in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Stone tools came first, then bronze (a mix of copper and tin), then iron. The Romans invaded in AD 43.
items.hook: Tools got tougher: **stone**, then **bronze**, then **iron**. Then the Romans arrived in AD 43.
items.example: Stone Age Skara Brae (Orkney) and Iron Age hillforts such as Maiden Castle (Dorset) can still be visited.

items.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items.explain: After the Romans left (c. 410), Anglo-Saxons settled. Vikings first raided in 793. The Normans conquered in 1066.
items.hook: “**R**omans **A**lways **V**isit **N**ormandy”: Romans, Anglo-Saxons, Vikings, Normans.
items.example: Hadrian’s Wall (Roman), Sutton Hoo (Anglo-Saxon), Jorvik in York (Viking), the Tower of London (Norman).

items.prompt: Put these periods in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Normans, then (after many medieval kings) the Tudors, Stuarts, Georgians and Victorians.
items.hook: “**N**o **T**iny **S**quirrel **G**ets **V**exed”: Normans, Tudors, Stuarts, Georgians, Victorians.
items.example: Hampton Court Palace has Tudor rooms built for Henry VIII and grand Stuart rooms added for William and Mary.

items.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Hastings 1066, Magna Carta 1215, the Black Death 1348, Bosworth (the first Tudor king) 1485.
items.hook: Picture them in order: an **arrow** (Hastings), a **charter** (Magna Carta), a **flea** (Black Death), a **crown** (Bosworth).
items.example: Original copies of the 1215 Magna Carta can be seen at the British Library in London.

items.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Armada 1588 (Elizabeth I), Gunpowder Plot 1605 (James I), Great Fire 1666 (Charles II), Victoria crowned 1838.
items.hook: “Remember, remember the fifth of November, gunpowder, treason and plot” (1605).
items.example: Bonfire Night (5 November) and the Monument in London, built for the Great Fire, still remind us of these events.

items.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items.explain: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC, the first recorded Olympics were in 776 BC, the Romans arrived in AD 43 and the House of Wisdom flourished in the 800s.
items.hook: The pyramids were already about **1800 years old** when the first Olympic Games were held.
items.example: The flame for every modern Olympic Games is still lit at Olympia in Greece.

items.prompt: In which year did the Romans invade Britain under Emperor Claudius?
items.explain: Julius Caesar visited in 55 and 54 BC, but the real invasion came in AD 43 under Claudius.
items.hook: Claudius sent **4** legions in AD **4**3: four legions, forty-three.
items.example: Hadrian’s Wall still stands across northern England; Watling Street is the line of today’s A5.

items.prompt: Roughly when did Roman rule in Britain end?
items.explain: Around AD 410 the Roman army left and Britain had to defend itself.
items.hook: 43 in, 410 out: the Romans ruled Britain for **nearly 370 years**.
items.example: The Roman Baths in Bath are still fed by the hot spring. The Romans called the town Aquae Sulis.

items.prompt: The first famous Viking raid hit the monastery at Lindisfarne. In which year?
items.explain: Vikings attacked Lindisfarne in 793, shocking Christian Europe.
items.hook: “Seven-nine-three, raiders from the sea.”
items.example: Lindisfarne (Holy Island) in Northumberland can only be reached across a causeway when the tide is out.

items.prompt: In which year was the Battle of Hastings?
items.explain: The Battle of Hastings was on 14 October 1066.
items.hook: 1066 → 1666 (Great Fire of London) is exactly **600 years**: just swap the 0 for a 6.
items.example: The town of Battle in East Sussex is named after it; Battle Abbey stands where the fighting took place.

items.prompt: In which year did King John agree to Magna Carta?
items.explain: Magna Carta (1215) limited the king’s power: even the king had to obey the law.
items.hook: “Twelve-fifteen, the barons were keen.”
items.example: Four 1215 copies survive: two at the British Library, one at Lincoln Castle and one at Salisbury Cathedral.

items.prompt: In which year did the Black Death reach England?
items.explain: The Black Death arrived in 1348 and killed perhaps a third to a half of the population.
items.hook: Black Death **1348**, Peasants’ Revolt **1381**: the revolt came 33 years later.
items.example: Builders of London’s Elizabeth line found a 1348 plague burial ground at Charterhouse Square in 2013.

items.prompt: Which family ruled England from 1485 to 1603?
items.explain: Henry VII became the first Tudor king after winning at Bosworth in 1485. The last Tudor was Elizabeth I, who died in 1603.
items.hook: Tudors: **1485** (Bosworth) to **1603** (Elizabeth I dies): five monarchs in 118 years.
items.example: Henry VIII’s warship, the Mary Rose, can be seen in Portsmouth; Hampton Court was one of his palaces.

items.prompt: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 until which year?
items.explain: Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901: over 63 years.
items.hook: Victoria lived just into the 20th century: she died in January **1901**.
items.example: Victorian post boxes still in use have “VR” on them: Victoria Regina (Queen Victoria).

items.prompt: In which years was the First World War?
items.explain: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918.
items.hook: **MAIN** causes of WW1: **M**ilitarism, **A**lliances, **I**mperialism, **N**ationalism. It ended at 11 a.m. on 11/11/1918.
items.example: On Remembrance Day (11 November) people wear poppies, which grew on the old battlefields of France and Belgium.

items.prompt: In which years was the Second World War?
items.explain: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945.
items.hook: WW2 began 21 years after WW1 ended: 1918 + 21 = **1939**. It lasted six years, to **1945**.
items.example: HMS Belfast, a Second World War warship, is moored on the Thames in London and can be visited.

items.prompt: Bronze is made by mixing copper with which metal?
items.explain: Bronze is copper mixed with tin. It was harder than copper alone.
items.hook: **C**opper + **T**in = bronze. Cornwall’s tin was traded far and wide in the Bronze Age.
items.example: Many statues, such as the four lions in Trafalgar Square, are cast in bronze.

items.prompt: Stonehenge was first built during which period?
items.explain: Work on Stonehenge began around 3000 BC, in the New Stone Age (Neolithic), and continued into the Bronze Age.
items.hook: **Stone**henge was begun in the **Stone** Age, around 3000 BC.
items.example: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, lines up with the sunrise on midsummer’s day.

items.prompt: Which Anglo-Saxon king of Wessex fought off the Vikings and is called “the Great”?
items.explain: Alfred the Great (king 871–899) defended Wessex against the Vikings.
items.hook: Alfred and the cakes: legend says that while hiding from the Vikings he let a woman’s cakes burn.
items.example: A huge statue of Alfred stands in Winchester, his capital; the Alfred Jewel is in Oxford’s Ashmolean Museum.

items.prompt: Which river did Ancient Egypt depend on?
items.explain: The Nile flooded every year, leaving rich soil for farming.
items.hook: “Egypt is the gift of the Nile”: the Greek writer Herodotus.
items.example: Egyptian mummies and coffins can be seen in the British Museum in London.

items.prompt: Mesopotamia means “land between two rivers”. Which two?
items.explain: Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) lay between the Tigris and Euphrates. The Sumerians there invented one of the first writing systems, cuneiform.
items.hook: **Meso** = middle, **potamos** = river: the land in the middle of the rivers. **T**igris and **E**uphrates: **T**wo **E**normous rivers.
items.example: Our 60-minute hour and 360° circle come from Mesopotamian counting in 60s.

items.prompt: Which civilisation built the planned cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro?
items.explain: The Indus Valley civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BC) had well-planned cities with drains.
items.hook: **Indus** → **India**: the river gave the country its name.
items.example: Mohenjo-daro had covered drains about 4500 years ago, thousands of years before London had sewers.

items.prompt: Which Chinese dynasty left writing on “oracle bones”?
items.explain: The Shang Dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC) carved questions to their gods on oracle bones.
items.hook: Shang priests heated **oracle bones** until they cracked, then read the cracks as the gods’ answers.
items.example: Some Chinese characters still look like their Shang ancestors, such as 人 (person) and 日 (sun).

items.prompt: What were Ancient Egyptian picture symbols for writing called?
items.explain: Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs. The Rosetta Stone helped scholars decode them in 1822.
items.hook: **Hiero** = holy, **glyph** = carving: hieroglyphs are “holy carvings”.
items.example: The Rosetta Stone, the key to reading hieroglyphs, is in the British Museum in London.

items.prompt: Which Greek city-state is famous for developing democracy?
items.explain: Athens developed democracy (“rule by the people”) around 508 BC, though only free men could vote.
items.hook: **Demos** = people, **kratos** = power: democracy is “people power”.
items.example: Every UK general election, when adults vote for their MP, uses the idea Athens began.

items.prompt: Which Greek city-state was famous for its warriors and tough training?
items.explain: Spartan boys began military training at about age 7.
items.hook: We still call something plain and tough “**spartan**”, after Sparta.
items.example: A bare room with hardly any furniture is still described as “spartan”.

items.prompt: In which year were the first recorded Olympic Games held?
items.explain: The first recorded Olympics were held at Olympia in 776 BC in honour of Zeus.
items.hook: **776 BC**: the Olympics are older than Rome, which legend says was founded in 753 BC.
items.example: London has hosted the modern Olympic Games three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

items.prompt: At which battle in 490 BC did the Athenians defeat the Persians?
items.explain: Legend says a runner ran from Marathon to Athens with the news, which is where the race gets its name.
items.hook: The marathon race is named after the legend of a runner carrying news of the victory to Athens.
items.example: The London Marathon, run every year, is 26.2 miles long.

items.prompt: Which of these do we owe to the Ancient Greeks?
items.explain: The Greeks gave us the Olympics, democracy, theatre and many words, such as “alphabet” (from alpha, beta).
items.hook: **Alphabet** = alpha + beta, the first two Greek letters.
items.example: The front of the British Museum copies the columns of an ancient Greek temple.

items.prompt: What was the name of the great centre of learning in Baghdad around AD 900?
items.explain: The House of Wisdom gathered scholars who translated and improved Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge.
items.hook: The **House of Wisdom**: a giant library where scholars translated books from Greek, Persian and Indian.
items.example: Our digits 0 to 9 reached Europe through scholars in the Islamic world, which is why we call them Arabic numerals.

items.prompt: The word “algebra” comes from the work of which Baghdad scholar?
items.explain: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) wrote a book whose title gave us “algebra”. The word “algorithm” comes from his name.
items.hook: His book “al-jabr” → **algebra**; his name, al-Khwarizmi → **algorithm**.
items.example: Every computer and app runs on algorithms: a word named after al-Khwarizmi.

items.prompt: What shape was the city of Baghdad when it was founded in 762?
items.explain: Caliph al-Mansur built Baghdad as a “Round City” with walls in a circle.
items.hook: Picture a giant coin: the Round City had the caliph’s palace and great mosque in the very centre.

items.prompt: The Maya civilisation was in which part of the world?
items.explain: The Maya lived in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize. Their classic period was about AD 250–900.
items.hook: **M**aya, **M**exico: southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, in Central America.
items.example: Maya pyramids, such as those at Chichén Itzá in Mexico, are visited by millions of people every year.

items.prompt: The Maya used a symbol for which important number, long before Europe?
items.explain: The Maya counted in 20s and had a symbol for zero, shaped like a shell.
items.hook: The Maya zero looked like a shell: an empty shell means nothing.
items.example: Without a zero you could not write 10, 100 or 2026: every calculator depends on it.

items.prompt: The Maya wrote using what?
items.explain: Maya writing used hundreds of glyphs carved on stone and written in folding books (codices).
items.hook: Glyphs, like Egyptian hiero**glyphs**: picture-signs carved in stone.
items.example: The Dresden Codex, one of the few Maya folding books to survive, is kept in a library in Dresden, Germany.

items.prompt: The Kingdom of Benin was in which modern country?
items.explain: The historic Kingdom of Benin was in what is now southern Nigeria, not the modern country called Benin.
items.hook: The Kingdom of Benin is **N**ot in Benin: it was in **N**igeria.
items.example: Benin City is still a large city in southern Nigeria, in West Africa.

items.prompt: What are the famous metal plaques and sculptures from Benin called?
items.explain: The Benin Bronzes are thousands of brass and bronze artworks. British soldiers took many in 1897.
items.hook: **B**enin **B**ronzes: many are really made of **b**rass.
items.example: Benin Bronzes are in the British Museum; some museums have now returned theirs to Nigeria.

items.prompt: What was the title of the ruler of Benin?
items.explain: The Oba ruled Benin from a great palace in Benin City.
items.hook: **Oba** for Benin, **Pharaoh** for Egypt, **Caliph** for Baghdad.
items.example: There is still an Oba of Benin today, with a palace in Benin City.

items.prompt: Why was there a fight for the throne in 1066?

options.text: Edward the Confessor died without a child to inherit
The Vikings had killed the whole royal family
options.feedback: No: the problem was that King Edward had no son or daughter.

options.text: England had never had a king before
options.feedback: England had had kings for over 100 years.

items.explain: King Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 with no children, so several men claimed the throne.
items.hook: No child, no clear heir: so a crowd of claimants, Harold, William, Harald and Edgar.
items.example: Edward the Confessor rebuilt Westminster Abbey and is buried there; monarchs are still crowned in it.

items.prompt: Who won the Battle of Hastings?

options.feedback: Hardrada was killed earlier at Stamford Bridge.

items.explain: William of Normandy defeated and killed Harold Godwinson on 14 October 1066.
items.hook: **W** for **W**illiam, **W** for **W**inner: he became William the Conqueror.
items.example: The Bayeux Tapestry, about 70 metres long, tells the story. Its home is a museum in Bayeux, Normandy.

items.prompt: Which English earl was crowned king the day after Edward the Confessor died?
items.explain: Harold Godwinson, the most powerful earl in England, was crowned on 6 January 1066.
items.hook: Harold was hasty: crowned the very **next day**, 6 January 1066.
items.example: Waltham Abbey in Essex claims to be Harold’s burial place; a stone marks the spot.

items.prompt: Which Norwegian king invaded northern England in September 1066?
items.explain: Harald Hardrada landed with Tostig, Harold’s exiled brother.
items.hook: “Hardrada” means roughly “hard ruler” in Old Norse: Norway’s tough Viking king.

items.prompt: Where did Harold defeat Harald Hardrada in September 1066?
items.explain: Harold marched north and won at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.
items.hook: Stamford Bridge is often called the **end of the Viking Age** in England.
items.example: Stamford Bridge is a real village east of York, with a memorial to the battle.

items.prompt: At which battle did Hardrada defeat the northern earls, before Stamford Bridge?
items.explain: Hardrada beat the earls Edwin and Morcar at Fulford, near York, on 20 September 1066.
items.hook: “**F**ish **S**wim **H**ome”: **F**ulford, **S**tamford Bridge, **H**astings, the three battles in order.

items.prompt: On what date was the Battle of Hastings?
items.explain: Hastings: 14 October 1066. William was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.
items.hook: Hastings 14/10/1066, then a **Christmas Day** coronation for William: 25/12/1066.
items.example: Battle Abbey marks where Harold fell; re-enactments of the battle are often held there in October.

items.prompt: Which teenage Anglo-Saxon prince also had a claim to the throne in 1066?
items.explain: Edgar Ætheling was the closest blood relative of Edward, but at about 14 he had little support.
items.hook: **Ætheling** means “prince”: Edgar was the royal boy hardly anyone backed.

items.prompt: Historians argue about why William won at Hastings. Which factor do most see as the MOST important?

options.text: Harold’s army was exhausted after marching north to Stamford Bridge and back
options.feedback: Strong choice: Harold’s men had marched about 400 km in under three weeks. Many historians put this first, alongside William’s tactics.

options.text: William’s tactics, including the feigned retreats that broke the shield wall
options.feedback: Strong choice: the Norman feigned retreats lured the English off the hill. Many historians put this first.

options.text: William had a papal banner from the Pope
options.feedback: This boosted morale and gave William’s cause legitimacy, but it didn’t win the battle on its own.

options.text: The weather was sunny that day
options.feedback: There’s no evidence the weather decided the battle. The wind direction mattered for when William could cross the Channel, not for the fighting.

items.explain: There is no single right answer: historians weigh Harold’s exhausted army, William’s tactics and luck (the wind delaying William until Harold had gone north). A strong answer compares factors and explains why one mattered most.

items.prompt: The Bayeux Tapestry was made for William’s half-brother, Bishop Odo. Which question could it BEST help a historian answer?

options.text: How did the Normans want people to remember the conquest?
What did ordinary English farmers think about William?
options.feedback: It was made for the Norman side, so it tells us little about English farmers’ views.

options.text: Exactly how many soldiers fought at Hastings?
options.feedback: It is an embroidery, not a record of numbers.

items.explain: Every source can be useful: a Norman-made source is excellent evidence of the Norman point of view.
items.hook: Ask **who made it, and why**: a Norman-made tapestry shows the Norman side.
items.example: A full-size Victorian copy of the Bayeux Tapestry is on show in Reading Museum.

items.prompt: What kind of castle did the Normans build quickly after 1066?
items.explain: A motte (earth mound) with a wooden tower, and a bailey (enclosed yard). Later many were rebuilt in stone.
items.hook: **M**otte = **M**ound; **B**ailey = **B**ig yard.
items.example: Clifford’s Tower in York stands on the motte William built in 1068; you can climb up to it today.

items.prompt: In which year was the Domesday survey carried out?
items.explain: William ordered the Domesday survey in 1086 to find out who owned what, so he could collect taxes.
items.hook: Domesday came 20 years after Hastings: 10**6**6 → 10**8**6.
items.example: You can search the Domesday Book online to see whether your town or village is in it.

items.prompt: Why did William order the Domesday Book?
items.answer: to find out what land was worth, for taxes
distractors: to record the soldiers who fought at Hastings
to write down all the laws of England
to list the books in every monastery
items.explain: Domesday recorded land, people, animals and value, showing William exactly what he could tax.
items.hook: It was nicknamed after **Doomsday**, Judgement Day: like God’s judgement, its answers could not be argued with.
items.example: The original Domesday Book is kept at The National Archives in Kew, London.

items.prompt: What was the system called where the king gave land in return for loyalty and military service?
items.explain: Under the feudal system, land passed down from king to barons to knights to peasants, with loyalty and service owed upward.
items.hook: Picture a pyramid: the **king** at the top, then **barons**, **knights**, and lots of **peasants** at the bottom.
items.example: Titles such as “baron” and “lord”, still used in the House of Lords, come from feudal times.

items.prompt: What do we call William’s brutal destruction of villages and crops in the north in 1069–70?
items.explain: After rebellions in the north, William’s soldiers destroyed homes, crops and animals; many thousands starved.
items.hook: To **harry** means to attack again and again: William harried the North to stop it rebelling.
items.example: The Domesday Book, 16 years later, still lists many Yorkshire villages as “waste”.

items.prompt: Which famous London castle was begun by William the Conqueror?
items.explain: The White Tower at the Tower of London was begun by William around 1078.
items.hook: The **White Tower**: William’s great stone keep, named after it was whitewashed in 1240.
items.example: The Tower of London is where the Crown Jewels are kept today.

items.prompt: Which language did the Norman rulers speak?
items.explain: The new rulers spoke Norman French, which is why English has pairs like cow (English) and beef (from French boeuf).
items.hook: Animals in the field have English names; meat on the Norman table has French ones: cow/beef, pig/pork, sheep/mutton.
items.example: The royal coat of arms still says “Dieu et mon droit”: French for “God and my right”.

items.prompt: Which great building in Durham did the Normans begin in 1093?
items.explain: Durham Cathedral is one of the finest Norman buildings, with huge round arches.
items.hook: Norman = **round** arches and fat pillars. Later Gothic churches have **pointed** arches.
items.example: Durham Cathedral is a World Heritage Site; its huge patterned pillars are over 900 years old.

items.prompt: Which change after 1066 affected the MOST people in England?

options.text: Almost all land passed from English to Norman lords
options.feedback: Strong: new lords meant new rent, new rules and new masters for millions of peasants.

options.text: New cathedrals were built in the Norman style
options.feedback: Impressive, but daily life for most people changed more because of new lords.

options.text: Kings now spoke French at court
options.feedback: This mattered for nobles and law, but most peasants never went to court.

items.explain: Think about scale: who was affected, and how deeply? The transfer of land touched nearly everyone.
